13.text: Snow-House. — The vaulted snow-house, which is typical for the Eskimo

14.text: tribes, does not occur anywhere on the Asiatic coast. Of all the tribes of

15.text: northeastern Asia, only the Kerek, who have no sufficient supply of wood or

16.text: skins to construct adequate winter houses, utilize snow as building-material.

17.text: Their half-underground house has a frame roughly constructed of such poles

18.text: and pieces of wood as they can find on the shore. Crooked branches of

19.text: stunted willow and birch trees are placed between to fill in the spaces, and

20.text: the whole is lined, from within with such skins as they can scrape together,

21.text: and from without with sod and loose earth. A long, low, narrow passage

22.text: made of similar material forms the entrance. It is divided into three parts,

23.text: closed by skin curtains. This structure is used in spring and summer as it

24.text: is; but in the fall it is covered with a thick layer of snow several feet deep,

25.text: and fashioned into a well-defined round or rectangular form, which gives to

26.text: this house some outward likeness to the Eskimo snow-house.

27.text: The interior arrangements are much like those of the houses of other

28.text: branches of the Maritime Koryak. The lack of a roof-entrance with its cha-

29.text: racteristic tree-ladder, however, gives it a peculiar feature. On that part of the

30.text: shore no logs fit for the purpose can be found. Thus the use of the tree-

31.text: ladder ceases suddenly on this part of the Asiatic shore for want of material.

32.text: Farther to the northward and eastward, across Bering Strait, along the American

33.text: shore on the Arctic and Pacific Oceans, are found various types of houses.

34.text: Still farther to the south, in America, after the forest border is reached again,

35.text: the square roof-entrance and the notched tree-ladder re-appear in exactly the

36.text: same shapes as among the Koryak and Kamchadal in Asia.

37.text: Cellars and Boat Supports. — Underground cellars were and are used

38.text: in all Chukchee villages for storing provisions. They also have supports

39.text: made of bone of the whale in their walls, and the entrance consists often of

40.text: a square frame with a shoulder-blade cover. Sometimes a vacant underground

41.text: house is used for a cellar.¹
